summary: A yes/no question has the same word order as the statement. In speech, rising intonation alone makes it a question (אַתָּה רוֹצֶה עַגְבָנִיָּה?); in writing and careful speech the particle הַאִם can open it (הַאִם אַתָּה רוֹצֶה עַגְבָנִיָּה?). There is no inversion and no auxiliary like English “do”. Answer with כֵּן or לֹא — or simply repeat the verb (— אַתָּה רוֹצֶה? — רוֹצֶה).

askYourself: Is it everyday speech? → keep the statement and raise your voice at the end (write “?”).
Is it formal or written? → put הַאִם at the very beginning.
Did I change the word order? → don’t: Hebrew questions keep the statement order.
Do I need a word for “do / does”? → no, Hebrew has none.

traps: No inversion and no “do”: “Do you want a tomato?” = אַתָּה רוֹצֶה עַגְבָנִיָּה?
הַאִם is formal; in conversation it can sound stiff.
Do not confuse הַאִם (question particle) with אִם (“if”).
A question by intonation alone is shown in writing only by the question mark — don’t forget it.

seeAlso.note: Arabic opens a yes/no question with هَلْ or أَ — the counterpart of the formal הַאִם.
German puts the verb first (Willst du …?) and answers a negative question with doch; Hebrew keeps the statement order.
Chinese adds 吗 at the end or uses A-not-A (要不要); Hebrew uses only intonation or הַאִם.
